title: Who Woke the Baby?
opening_frame: Two rival babysitters reach for the last slice of pizza beside a sleeping baby. One points to their handwritten agreement: “Wake the baby = diaper duty.”
question_and_goals: Who can get the slice without taking responsibility for the impending diaper change? Each sitter wants the food and wants the other to make the noise.
rule: Their own agreement assigns the chore to the person who wakes the baby. It is an agreement between these two characters, not a magical rule binding the returning parent.
causal_escalation: One places a squeaky toy in the other's path; the other catches the first person's vibrating phone and holds it over the toy. A wobbling plate forces both to catch it. Each attempt to trap the rival leaves the pair sharing a more precarious, silent pose. At midpoint, neither can move without noise, so they must cooperate. They hear the parent's jingling keys, exchange a look and silently clear the noisy objects from the entrance, finally choosing to protect the baby's sleep together.
plant_and_payoff: The keys are heard before the parent appears; the diaper bag has been visible throughout. The parent arrives, sees the unusually quiet teamwork, and whispers, “Great. You're both free.” The diaper bag lands between them. They exchange a defeated look, split the pizza and take the bag together. They got the food and ended the feud, but their clever private rule never excused them from the job.
visual_test: Keep the baby safe and comfortable; the adults' ridiculous self-entanglement supplies the comedy. This needs distinct personalities and a clean final shared choice, otherwise it is only a string of hush gestures.
editorial_note: These are pitches, not approved productions or timed boards. Together with the three fully boarded films above, they make eight topics. They should be developed only if their central visual test works; a striking premise is not yet a finished film.

source.section: Five more distinct topics: an eight-story development slate
